lead: A feedback loop rarely lands exactly on the commanded value. The wobble dies away, but a small offset often stays: the steady-state error, e<sub>ss</sub>. It matters wherever tracking accuracy is the whole point — a servomotor holding an antenna angle, a temperature loop settling at its set point, a payment gateway settling its output. Three numbers, Kp, Kv and Ka, read straight off the open-loop transfer function, and the system type picks which one applies.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.2 for type, Chapter 2.1 for the standard inputs, and the final value theorem from Laplace transforms.

sections.h3: The error signal and the final value theorem

blocks.text: In a unity negative feedback loop the summing node subtracts C(s) from R(s) to give the error: E(s) = R(s) − C(s). The forward path gives C(s) = G(s)E(s). Substituting and rearranging:

blocks.where: E(s) is the Laplace transform of the error at the comparator; R(s) is the transform of the reference input; G(s) is the open-loop forward-path transfer function, including the plant and any controller.

blocks.text: The steady-state error is e(t) as t → ∞. The final value theorem avoids the inverse transform: multiply E(s) by s and take s → 0.
e<sub>ss</sub> = lim<sub>t→∞</sub> e(t) = lim<sub>s→0</sub> s E(s) = lim<sub>s→0</sub> s R(s) / (1 + G(s))
blocks.where: e<sub>ss</sub> is the steady-state error; the equality holds only if every pole of sE(s) lies in the left half of the s-plane, which in practice means the closed loop must be stable.

blocks.text: That condition is not decoration. An unstable closed loop never settles, so 'steady-state error' has no meaning. Confirm stability first — Unit 3, Stability and Root Locus — and only then apply the theorem.

Feed each standard input into the limit and the G(s) terms separate. For a unit step R(s) = 1/s, so sR(s) = 1 and e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/(1 + lim G(s)). For a unit ramp R(s) = 1/s², giving 1/lim sG(s). For a unit parabola R(s) = 1/s³, giving 1/lim s²G(s). Name the three limits once and every system is covered.
Kp = lim<sub>s→0</sub> G(s),   Kv = lim<sub>s→0</sub> s G(s),   Ka = lim<sub>s→0</sub> s² G(s)
blocks.where: Kp is the static position error constant; Kv is the static velocity error constant, with unit s⁻¹; Ka is the static acceleration error constant, with unit s⁻². All three are computed from the open-loop G(s), never from the closed-loop transfer function.

blocks.text: e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/(1 + Kp)  for unit step,   1/Kv for unit ramp,   1/Ka for unit parabola
blocks.where: the step error is dimensionless; a ramp of slope A gives A/Kv; a parabola of value A t²/2 gives A/Ka. A constant multiplier A on the input multiplies the error by the same A.

blocks.text: The constants come out finite, zero or infinite according to how many poles G(s) has at the origin — the system type, as defined in Chapter 2.2. A factor sN cancels the s and s² of the limits for N = 1 and N = 2, which is exactly why integrators remove error.

sections.h3: Type, input and the error table

blocks.text: Read the table as a ladder. Each extra pole at the origin knocks out one more column. Type 0 cannot follow a ramp: the output falls further and further behind. Type 1 follows a step exactly but trails a ramp by a constant lag of 1/Kv. Type 2 follows both exactly and lags only a parabola.

Climbing the ladder costs stability. Each pole at the origin adds 90° of phase lag, swinging the root locus towards the right half plane and shrinking the usable gain. Add an integrator to kill error, then pay with poorer damping and slower recovery. Unit 5 shows the PI and PID controllers that do this deliberately.

With non-unity feedback the comparator sees E = R − H·C and E(s) = R(s)/(1 + G(s)H(s)). Use the loop gain GH in place of G in all three constants. Some syllabi say 'static error coefficients'; others say 'error constants'. Same quantities.

figure.caption: The comparator forms the error E(s) from the input and the fed-back output; with unity feedback the fed-back signal is C(s) itself, so E(s) = R(s)/(1 + G(s)).

spec.aria: A block diagram of a unity feedback loop in which the input and the fed-back output meet at the summing node to form the error E of s, which drives G of s.

examples.question: A unity feedback system has open-loop transfer function G(s) = 100/[s(s + 10)]. Find the steady-state error for a unit step, a unit ramp and a unit parabola input. State the system type first.
steps: G(s) = 100/[s(s + 10)] has one pole at the origin, so the type is 1.
Kp = lim s→0 G(s) = ∞ because of the 1/s factor, so step error = 1/(1 + Kp) = 0.
Kv = lim s→0 s G(s) = 100/10 = 10 s⁻¹, so ramp error = 1/Kv = 0.1.
Ka = lim s→0 s² G(s) = 0, so parabola error = 1/0 = ∞: the output never catches a parabola.
examples.answer: Type 1 system: step error = 0, ramp error = 0.1, parabola error = ∞.
examples.check:
K = 100.0
a = 10.0
Kv = K / a
ess_step = 0.0
ess_ramp = 1.0 / Kv
print("step error =", ess_step)
print("Kv =", Kv)
print("ramp error =", ess_ramp)

examples.question: A unity feedback system has G(s) = 50/(s + 5) and is driven by a step of size 5. Find the steady-state error.
steps: G(s) has no pole at the origin, so the type is 0.
Unit-step error = 1/(1 + Kp) = 1/11 ≈ 0.0909. The input size A = 5 scales it: e<sub>ss</sub> = 5/11 ≈ 0.4545.
The closed-loop pole is at s = −55, so the loop is stable and the number holds.
examples.answer: The steady-state error for the step of size 5 is 5/11 ≈ 0.455.
examples.check:
K = 50.0
a = 5.0
Kp = K / a
A = 5.0
ess = A / (1.0 + Kp)
print("Kp =", Kp)
print("step error =", ess)

traps: Evaluating Kp, Kv, Ka on the closed-loop transfer function C(s)/R(s) instead of the open-loop G(s). The constants are defined on G(s) only — using the closed loop gives wrong, often finite, answers.
Quoting a finite error for a system whose closed loop is unstable. The final value theorem needs every closed-loop pole in the left half plane; without that check the number is meaningless.
Mixing up Kp with the proportional-controller gain Kp of Unit 5. Here Kp is a limit of G(s) at s = 0; it is not a knob you turn.
Forgetting the input size A. A ramp of slope A gives A/Kv, not 1/Kv; a parabola of A t²/2 gives A/Ka, not 1/Ka.
Writing 1/0 = 0. A zero constant means infinite error, not zero error. Zero error comes from an infinite constant.

quiz.q: Define the three static error constants for a unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function G(s).
quiz.a: Kp = lim s→0 G(s); Kv = lim s→0 s G(s), unit s⁻¹; Ka = lim s→0 s² G(s), unit s⁻². All are limits of the open-loop G(s), and they give the steady-state error as 1/(1 + Kp), 1/Kv and 1/Ka for unit step, ramp and parabola.

quiz.q: Why does the final value theorem require the closed loop to be stable?
quiz.a: The theorem states that lim t→∞ e(t) equals lim s→0 sE(s) only if all poles of sE(s) lie in the left half plane. A right-half-plane closed-loop pole makes e(t) grow without bound, so no finite limit exists and the computed number describes nothing.

quiz.q: A unity feedback system has G(s) = 20/[s(s + 4)]. Find the steady-state error for a unit ramp.
quiz.a: One pole at the origin, so type 1. Kv = lim s→0 s·20/[s(s + 4)] = 20/4 = 5 s⁻¹. e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/Kv = 1/5 = 0.2. The output trails the unit ramp by 0.2 units.

quiz.q: A type 0 system has G(s) = 30/(s + 6) with unity feedback. Find the error for a step of size 4.
quiz.a: Kp = 30/6 = 5. Unit-step error = 1/(1 + 5) = 1/6. Scaling by A = 4 gives e<sub>ss</sub> = 4/6 ≈ 0.667. The closed-loop pole at s = −36 is stable, so the result holds.

quiz.q: Why does a type 2 system give zero error for both a step and a ramp?
quiz.a: The factor s² in the denominator cancels the s and s² that the limits introduce. Kp = lim G(s) is infinite and Kv = lim sG(s) is also infinite, so 1/(1 + Kp) and 1/Kv are both zero. Only Ka stays finite.

quiz.q: A control loop is type 0 and has a small but non-zero step error. A designer adds a pole at the origin. Discuss the effect on the error and on stability.
quiz.a: The system becomes type 1, so Kp becomes infinite and the step error falls to zero; the ramp error becomes finite at 1/Kv. But the added pole contributes 90° of phase lag at every frequency, pulling the root locus towards the right half plane and reducing the gain margin (Unit 4). The redesign must re-check stability and damping before accepting the zero error.

quiz.q: A loop has non-unity feedback with H(s) = 2 and G(s) = 50/(s + 5). What is the step error at the comparator?
quiz.a: Use the loop gain GH. At s → 0, GH → (50/5)·2 = 20, so the effective position constant is 20 and the comparator error is 1/(1 + 20) = 1/21 ≈ 0.0476 for a unit step. The output error R − C is a different quantity: C(∞) = G(0)·E = 10/21 ≈ 0.476, so R − C = 1 − 10/21 = 11/21 ≈ 0.524.

quiz.q: State the steady-state error of a type 0 system to a unit ramp input.
quiz.a: Infinite. Kv = lim s→0 sG(s) = 0 for a type 0 system, so e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/Kv = ∞. The output falls further and further behind a ramp.

beyond: Not for the exam. Servo-drive datasheets quote the velocity error constant in s⁻¹ as a tracking-stiffness figure. When the reference is not a step, ramp or parabola — a drone on a curved path — the constants give way to the dynamic error coefficients of Chapter 2.7. Modern drives add feedforward of the reference derivative so a type 1 axis tracks a ramp with almost no lag.
